title: Spurs outduel Thunder for epic Game 7 win, advance to NBA Finals
author: Jared Weiss
content:
The defending champs have been dethroned.

Facing a hostile crowd in Oklahoma City, the San Antonio Spurs showed no sign of nerves, using a balanced attack, excellent 3-point shooting and a stingy defense to pull out a 111-103 victory in Game 7 of the Western Conference finals Saturday night.

The Spurs now advance to the NBA Finals for a chance to win their sixth NBA championship — and the first since 2014. They’ll have to get past the New York Knicks to do so, with Game 1 set for Wednesday in San Antonio.

Victor Wembanyama, named the Western Conference finals MVP, had 22 points and seven rebounds, but the Spurs received contributions up and down their roster. De’Aaron Fox had perhaps his best game of the series, consistently hitting big shots to stop Thunder runs. He finished with 15 points, five assists and three steals.

Julian Champagnie scored 20 points and added six rebounds. Luke Kornet sparked a crucial four-point turnaround late in the game with a chase-down block of Oklahoma City’s Isaiah Hartenstein. Keldon Johnson hit a pair of huge 3-pointers in the fourth quarter and finished with 11 points.

OKC’s two-time reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander led all scorers with 35 points and also had nine assists, but it wasn’t enough to counter the varied Spurs attack.

Here are the takeaways from Saturday night’s Game 7.

What do you do when Wembanyama gets his fifth foul and the whole season is on the line?

Luke Kornet checked in for just two defensive possessions, looking like a Wemby on both of them. When Wembanyama came back in, Julian Champagnie missed him standing all alone under the hoop. Then, Dylan Harper came flying in for the put-back, just like Wemby would.

Every time the Thunder threatened to come back, the Spurs found someone to go above and beyond their role to make a huge play. Fox’s ankle has rendered him a shell of himself all series, then he comes out and has the most important game of his career.

That’s the beauty of this Spurs team: They are loaded with versatility and determination. Now they are heading to the NBA Finals, with a series comeback for the ages. — Jared Weiss, Spurs writer

When Oklahoma City had the upper hand in the West finals, it was still the team that could conjure more responses. It needed players that could hurtle toward Wembanyama without fear, and it summoned the quick trigger of Jared McCain. It needed defensive poise and disruption, and it found more from Alex Caruso and Cason Wallace.

It needed depth to supplement a forgettable series from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, and in moments, it did.

But San Antonio had the answers down the stretch of this seven-game series. It got an abundance of transition 3s and flourished from the corners during its hot starts. Luke Kornet’s minutes behind Wembanyama no longer felt like such a detriment. Its turnovers dwindled, with better control from its vaunted backcourt. Wembanyama more frequently channeled a version of him that could be considered the best player in the world.

The Spurs had all the responses necessary. As a result, their timeline as a juggernaut begins now. — Joel Lorenzi, Thunder writer

The general belief in the NBA is that the team that hits first is usually the one who wins — a saying that’s more metaphorical than it is literal. It speaks of force, of intent, of aggression.

In Game 7, the Spurs hit first in the most Thunder way possible. Victor Wembanyama drove to the corner, extended his arm, created space and hit a midrange jumper.

Saturday night, the Spurs were more Thunder than the defending champs. They were more aggressive getting to their spots. They better used their physicality. And, in the most surprising twist, they were more poised, handling every crowd chat, every Thunder run with maturity that they shouldn’t possess.

They did it from the start. They hit first. And the Thunder never really caught up. — Dan Woike, NBA writer
